# RG03 `deployer-is-attacker`: The exploit runs as the contract that deployed the protocol

<!-- Generated by `realism-gate explain --markdown`. Do not edit by hand. -->

**Severity:** warn (warn when a call is named like an access-controlled function; note for any other call the deployer makes)

The test contract deploys the code under review and then calls it without changing sender. A warning means one of those calls is named like an access-controlled function. A note means the calls are ordinary and this is the local-deployment pattern.

## Why it matters

Constructors commonly give the deployer ownership or every role. A test that deploys with `new Vault()` and then calls `vault.sweep()` from the test contract has proved that the deployer can sweep. A test that deploys locally and then calls `deposit` or `hash` has not: that is how almost every local harness is written, and reporting it as a warning buried the cases that matter. The warning is kept for the call whose name says it is gated. The note remains so the pattern is visible without failing a run that fails on warnings.

## How to fix it

Deploy and configure as one address, attack as another: `vm.startPrank(attacker)` before the exploit steps, or transfer ownership to a dedicated owner in `setUp()`. For a note, do that if any of the calls is in fact gated under a name the tool does not recognise, or silence it with an `allow` comment.

## Fires on

```solidity
function setUp() public { vault = new Vault(); }
function test_sweep() public {
    vault.sweep(address(token)); // runs as the deployer
}
```

## Does not fire on

```solidity
function setUp() public { vault = new Vault(); }
function test_sweep() public {
    vm.prank(attacker);
    vault.sweep(address(token));
}
```

## How it can be wrong

- A function that is gated but is not named like one (`harvest`, `skim`, `poke`). The finding is a note, and the gate is missed. Rename nothing; an `allow` comment is the wrong tool here, because the note is already the low severity. Say so in the report.
- A function that is named like a setter and is permissionless. The warning is wrong. Silence it with an `allow` comment that says the function is ungated.
- A constructor that hands ownership to an argument the tool does not read as privileged. Pass a variable named for the role (`owner`, `admin`) or the rule will not see the handover and will keep the deployer as the owner.

## In Solana tests (Rust and Anchor TypeScript)

The exploit's transactions are signed only by the keys that signed the setup, usually the harness's `payer` or Anchor's `provider.wallet` (which signs every `.rpc()`), and by no separate attacker keypair.

**How to fix it:** Set up as one keypair, attack as another: create an `attacker` keypair, fund it, and have it sign the exploit.

### Fires on

```rust
let (mut banks, payer, _) = program_test.start().await;
process(&mut banks, &[init_pool_ix(&payer.pubkey())], &[&payer]).await;
process(&mut banks, &[sweep_ix(&payer.pubkey())], &[&payer]).await;
```

```typescript
await program.methods.initPool().accounts({ payer: provider.wallet.publicKey }).rpc();
await program.methods.sweep().accounts({ recipient: provider.wallet.publicKey }).rpc();
```

### Does not fire on

```rust
process(&mut banks, &[init_pool_ix(&payer.pubkey())], &[&payer]).await;
let attacker = Keypair::new();
process(&mut banks, &[sweep_ix(&attacker.pubkey())], &[&payer, &attacker]).await;
```

```typescript
await program.methods.initPool().accounts({ payer: provider.wallet.publicKey }).rpc();
await program.methods.sweep().accounts({ recipient: attacker.publicKey }).signers([attacker]).rpc();
```

### Known false-positive modes

- A program with no access control, where the setup key gains nothing. The finding is a note when the instruction is not named like a gated call, and a warning when it is (`sweep`, `set_fee`). An `allow` comment is how to silence the warning.
- Setup the tool does not recognise as setup (no `init`- or `create`-style instruction name, no helper named `setup` or similar, no `before` hook or test titled for setup), which moves the start of the exploit earlier. Put the setup in a function named `setup`, or in a `before` hook.

## In Move tests (Sui and Aptos)

Not checked. Move unit tests have no Foundry cheatcode and this rule reads one, or it reads realism.yaml on its own. Privileged signers, admin caps, test-only mints, missing assertions and missing baselines are the Move checks.

## Silencing it

An `allow` comment in the repo under review does not silence this rule, and neither does a `realism.yaml` or `realism-gate.toml` inside that repo. Policy is an operator file outside the tree (`--declaration`, `--config`). `--trust-inline-allows` is the author switch, for a PoC you wrote and are not gating.

```solidity
// realism-gate: allow(RG03) <why this is not a defect here>
```

The comment is the same in Rust, TypeScript and Move. A comment without a reason is ignored even with `--trust-inline-allows`, and the output says so.
